utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please bring in the witness, please, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I believe we left off yesterday, if I'm correct - but you may remind me - discussing the maps which you were using to explain to the Court the situation in 1992, and I think we still had two maps which we had no time to go through, so that I would like to ask the usher to help us. ID D1/70, and ID D1/71. I think that the last map was -- you remember, we were looking at this map last, this. Now, the aftermath, the result of the war with the JNA, if you can explain it on the map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to repeat once again: Blue areas are the areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina controlled by the Croat Defence Council, the green areas are controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and these red areas were under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, we agreed to use this map without translation, but you have to ask some questions to indicate what is this map about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, will you also read to us this text in Croatian and give us also the number of the document so that Their Honours can follow.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The year is 1992, the month is June, and the map shows the directions of emigration, of movement of Muslims and Croats from the territory which we call the territory of Republika Srpska. The Serbs were expelling -- or rather, the population fled in the face of the crimes committed by that army, and a huge number of people - some point in time, over 400.000 - fled towards Croatia, taking different directions towards Croatia, and some Muslims remained in the territory controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was mentioned yesterday, and I will confirm it today, that the number of the expelled and refugees from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the territory of the Republic of Croatia exceeded 400.000, and as large a number of people - Muslims, Bosniaks - stayed in the territory controlled by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croat Defence Council. One of the reasons for the major tension and repeated tension in these territories between the Croats and the Muslims was, among other things, the fact that with the arrival of a large number of Muslims to towns populated before the war, inhabited before the war, by Croats and Muslims, the percentages may have varied, but now, it changed significantly the ethnic composition of those towns. A certain ethnic occupation took place, if I may call it that, of the lands, ethnic occupation by Muslims expelled by the Serbs. They took flats and houses, say in Mostar, flats that were formerly inhabited by Serbs who had left Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but Mr. Praljak, do you know how many flats are involved and how many were taken, of course if you know any figures?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not be able to give you those figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But would you know an approximate figure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But it would be several thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean several thousand flats?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. In particular, after the fall of Jajce and all the Muslim population from the area of Banja Luka and this part here, the ethnic structure was changed in Central Bosnian towns, where the number of Muslims grew to one to five, one to six, one to seven, in relation to Croats. The towns concerned are Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, Novi Travnik, Travnik, and so and so forth. And that gave rise to additional tension in those areas, because people who had been expelled were very, in a manner of speaking, aggressive. They behaved aggressively in the places that they came to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I will now show you a map which is ID D1/72 -- no, excuse me, we have another map, a different map on the screen. Do you wish to comment on this one, too?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are figures. The year is 1992, and it is November of 1992, and the map shows the number of expelled Muslims and Croats. And these figures apply only to the period after the fall of Jajce. The fall of Jajce produced --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel. Mr. President, these dates and figures, if we could have some foundation, please, as to the source of this information, what it's based on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Please indicate once again which map. Is it ID D1/72?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, ID D1/72 -- no, sorry, 71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may ask some questions concerning about some foundations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You've heard the Prosecution's objection. You heard His Honour. Can you tell us on what facts were these maps and these figures included?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the facts, the information we collected from the bureau for the expelled persons and escaped persons of the Croats. I personally participated in the organisation of the Croats and their transfer towards the Republic of Croatia. And also another information is the size of the population, the overall number of the population, in Jajce, before, in October, 1992, it fell into the Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I thank you very much. Mr. Praljak, I would also like to ask you only two or three questions more, and then we will move to another topic. Were you planning liberation actions in this area with the army of BH? Were there any instructions from the army of BH: Who was entrusted with the defence of Mostar? Who was responsible for the defence of Mostar? This will be in this group of several questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Usher will you please put this map on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please read the number down there and it is ID D1/72. And then will you please tell the Court what this map is about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the first question, the cooperation with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I could tell you first about June, 1992, about the liberation of Mostar, which started with the liberation of Boksevica, an important vantage point above Mostar on the right bank of the Neretva. That operation of the liberation of Boksevica was conducted by Mr. Mladen Naletilic. In view of its success and the situation on the ground, I took over the command, and we, the Croat Defence Council, that's by the evening that same day, reached the right bank of the Neretva. A few days later, I ordered independently the crossing of the Neretva River, together with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which did not commit a particularly large number of their troops in that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you give us the number of the troops?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first night of the attack, the number of their soldiers who crossed to the left bank of the Neretva was between 30 and 40. I know this figure because I requested a precise report from their commander, whom I knew by his nickname, which was Tetak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us something about the destruction in Mostar -- no. When we come to that topic. I'm sorry. When we come to the summer of 1993. But rather, Mr. Praljak, you said yesterday - maybe there was some confusion. Yesterday that you said Mr. Naletilic took part in the liberation of Orlovac, today you said Boksevica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm terribly sorry. I was completely off the map today. Orlovac, not Boksevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You said that yesterday in your testimony. Boksevica is a completely different hill, in a completely different area.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Such confusions can happen. Orlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us, were the bridges mined? Was there any destruction? Which area did you liberate in that action? I mean, which part of Mostar did you liberate, I mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the order of General Perisic, there are exact -- the exact names of men who, in a single day, blew up all the bridges over the Neretva. This was done by an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, a Croat from Dalmacija. Six bridges were blown up in one day, because in them -- in the structure of those bridges --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean at the time when the bridges were built?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the bridges were built, they were in them places -- let me explain. Whenever a bridge was built in Yugoslavia, it was designed so that room was left there for an explosive charge which, in case of a military need, would easily be put there and the bridge could then fall down according to statistic calculations. And in all the foundations on the Neretva -- in all the bridges over the Neretva, the explosive was already in place, and when the Yugoslav People's Army came to that area, it was then activated at the point when the Serbs decided that the left bank of the Neretva was their territory. The only bridge which was not demolished at that time was the old bridge in Mostar, but it was very badly damaged. Personally -- I personally issued the order to use very thick boards and put up a structure around the bridge so that mortar projectiles would not destroy it, and two soldiers of the Croat Defence Council were killed in the process. This structure protected the bridge for months, and there is a sufficient number of photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you said that the Serbs took the left bank of the Neretva before you set off to liberate it. If I told you that in this Court we heard a series of witnesses who testified to the following: that there was an agreement between the Serbs and the Croats that the Serbs should take the left bank, the Croats the right bank, and the Muslims would go into the Neretva, what would you say to that, since you were the commander of that operation, of the liberation of Mostar, in 1992, of course?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The absurdity of that thesis is best attested to by the action during which Capljina, Stolac, and the whole territory up to 15 or 20 kilometres above Mostar were liberated, and a large number of dead, of fallen soldiers of the Croat Defence Council and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina too who participated in that. If there was an understanding, then the whole action and all those dead are absurd. If there was such an action, if they were dead, then there was no such understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of such an understanding, of such an agreement, that there was an agreement to split Mostar, to partition Mostar in that way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And should you know such a thing, since you were a commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I should know such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, and what about the shelling in Mostar one day to the other? But tell us only about what is your personal knowledge. When it is not, then tell us, "I don't know it personally."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know personally not only that there was shelling, Mostar was set on fire by the Serbs. I personally know it also because after that I found, on my own, a thousand metres of Kodak film, negative, and a cameraman, and sent them to the left bank of the Neretva to take photographs to record what had been left after the Serb shelling and arson. That material, those films, were developed and then transferred to Beta videotapes, and this material is stored in the archives of the television in Zagreb, that is, the Croatian television, and it is in the archives of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and I also have it. It can be placed at the disposal whenever the Prosecution or the Defence or the Court want it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Praljak. We shall certainly need the tapes, so let me announce it in advance that we shall turn to you for assistance. But we still owe a commentary of this map, so could you do that briefly and then we shall move on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The joint planning of the liberation operations obstructed by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The year is 1992, November and December. I am not as familiar with this area here, that is, with Kupres, because that was not my area, but I know with certainty, because I participated in the planning of the liberation of some areas which were of technical importance for the town of Konjic. I can say that the Muslims and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, too, at that time were expressing certain reservation with regard to the cooperation with the Croat Defence Council, and voices, opinions, against the cooperation with the Croat Defence Council. Together with the commanders of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Konjic, together with General Miljenko Lasic of the Croat Defence Council, we planned an operation to push away the Serb forces from Konjic if -- so as to reduce the shelling considerably. For 48 hours -- sorry, 48 hours before the action began, the order from Sarajevo came that not only the mayor in Konjic should be dismissed but also the area military commanders there. So the action never even started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me about December, 1992. Were there any negotiations for the liberation of Sarajevo, negotiations to dovetail positions with the BH army? And if so, what was the result of them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, in June, or a little later, at the beginning of autumn, in a talk I had with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic in Mostar, I proposed the joint deblocking of Sarajevo. This was not accepted at that time. I know that negotiations were held afterwards with respect to a joint operation because at the time the HVO was a strong, powerful and fairly well-organised army, and it had a string of successes behind it. On our part, General Petkovic led those negotiations. I know about those negotiations, but, of course, he would be able to tell you more about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, let us go to December, 1992, and January, 1993. Were there any incidents that took place with the BH army? And as far as you know, how many soldiers did the BH army have, where were they concentrated, and was there any demarcation line with the Army of Republika Srpska in which they went into operation, if they did? And if they did not, tell us why, please. And then we will take a look at another map, which is ID D1/74.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It's okay. It's no problem. It's much easier, Madam Registrar. Much easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you read out what it says on the map for the Judges?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The year is 1992, and it is the period between the month of May and December, and shown here are the incidents that took place between the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO. Do you want me to go through them one by one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No, you don't have to do that. The document speaks for itself. I just wanted you to comment on a few of these incidents which you know Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about so that we can check out the document, confirm them or not, as the case may be.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally know about some of them because I went to try and bring about peace after they had taken place. As to the others, I know about them from the information I had at my disposal. As you can see, there were quite a lot of them. They were of a local character, and they very often depended on, if I can put it that way, the mood that prevailed between the two ethnic groups in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, not an objection but I just -- I assume everyone in the courtroom may have the same trouble we have. It's very impossible, really impossible, to read the detail on the map, the names, the dates and things. If it could be -- perhaps the booth could assist us if it can be better focused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Could we zoom in a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I provided the map. My colleague has just informed me that we took the copy we had intended for you to give to the Trial Chamber. [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we can see all the dates now where the occurrences took place and the years, or rather the year.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can comment Uskoplje, for example, on the 20th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were you there personally? Do you have personal, direct knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went there afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem is that the population was expelled by the Serbs from Donji Vakuf. This is Donji Vakuf here. And the Serbs renamed it and called it Serbograd or Serboslav, or one or the other, and the population was expelled, and it stayed on in Gornji Vakuf, largely. There were so many new people arriving into an area which had a well-balanced ethnic structure in Gornji Vakuf, which straight away created a whole series of problems. On the 20th of June, there was a major incident that took place, but the situation was quelled for a time. However, afterwards, as we moved into 1993, the situation escalated to become an all-out conflict. I myself was in Prozor immediately after this incident, and I held a whole series of negotiations with the commanders of the BH army, in an attempt to negotiate an agreement, together with them, and to look into the causes, the causes, and so find a solution to the situation, and so on and so forth. This would require an entire study, if we wanted to explain this map fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We have an opportunity now, when you're doing your direct examination of an important witness, to help the Trial Chamber. For two of us it's our first trial of events in the former Yugoslavia. You've been at pains for quite a long time to tell us that everybody spoke the same language and there was no such thing really as a Bosniak language, and as far as we can see, there is no visible difference in the appearance or dress between somebody of Muslim origin or Croat or Serb origin. Can you use the opportunity, please, to assist us in what caused the tensions between the parties? Did they eat different food? Did they have different customs? What was it? It's not quite literally a black-and-white issue. Perhaps you could assist us. I certainly would be very grateful for some assistance. Why would the arrival of additional Croats in a Muslim area or Muslims in a Croat area cause so much dissent, when you had a common enemy?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you have just heard the questions from Her Honour. Could you please assist the Trial Chamber and the Court in understanding what was going on, at least for December, 1992? And then we will move on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll do my best, although we have already had an interpretation of the war and why the war. Now, may I ask for your indulgence and a little patience for stepping outside the framework of these facts and figures?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is impossible to reduce everything to the matter of language, linguistics, manner of dress and food, Your Honour. It would be difficult to explain 90 per cent of the wars being waged in the world today in that way, and there were more than 17.000, if I'm correct, since ancient Greece. The Protestants against the Catholics is a case in point in Northern Ireland: The same people, the same culture, the same civilisation, and for years and years, tens of years, we see that the conflicts are persisting. And the same thing is true in our area or part of the world. At one point, a very precarious balance was upset. The war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a war between three nations, three ethnic groups, for two reasons: What the rights of peoples and individuals would look like in a state which would be born after all that; and who, in that part of the war, would defend the part of its territory or their territory which they considered to belong to them. In addition to this, let me also state the following. In the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, with half a million Croats who were down there and stayed on living there, seven and a half thousand people died of that half million. Now, may I give you the equivalent facts and figures? This resembles -- it would be as if, in America, four million people died. It would be the same ratio. It would be the same thing as if in -- as if 250.000 people were to be killed in the Netherlands, for example; the ratio would be the same. Or in China, if you had 17 million people killed or dead. In my opinion, one should conduct psychosociological studies to gorge the sentiments and feelings of the people after suffering so many casualties and having so many victims. Let me also mention that the number of victims on the Muslim side was no smaller. I think that their casualties were even greater, but not greater than the Croats. If we know that in the Second World War, 380.000 Americans lost their lives, then these figures, in my opinion, take on even greater proportions. It is difficult to imagine that any people can, through offensive operations, sustain such a large number of casualties and victims. So many victims fell -- the victims are high when the war has a civil character, ethnic character, and the character of a defence war as well. So that the question of language or linguistics is one part. Of course, people can think that they speak the same language, but we call that language Croatian and the Serbs call their language Serbian. The syntax -- in syntax and grammar, the syntax and grammar and the style, or stylistics, there are great differences between those languages. It is the right of Muslims, which has never been brought in question, to call themselves a nation and to have the language that they speak called the way they want to call it. That is their right. But of course it is also the right of the Croats not to accept that language, because they already have their own language. Now, the extent to which the Bosnian language or Bosniak language, or whatever they wish to call it, will take root and be accepted, I can't say, although I'm not actually a layman. I'm not quite a layman in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, according to your knowledge, your personal knowledge, to follow on from what Judge Clark just said, was it the war of a nation fighting for its territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only a battle for territory, Mr. Krsnik. The Serbs entered the war with the desire to take a portion of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least to the tune of 66 per cent of the territory, to take it away with them or to separate it and take it away into a state of its own, which can be called Yugoslavia, or Serbia, or Serbia and Montenegro, whichever. The Muslims, for their part, as early on as the Muslim declaration by Alija Izetbegovic and the premises it was founded upon, continuously believed that Bosnia-Herzegovina was their state, belonged to them, first and foremost, a state in which they were the founding or fundamental people, whereas the Croats and Serbs have their own reserve homelands, if I can put it that way. Now, if we exclude a portion of Croatian political thought, which experienced Bosnia-Herzegovina as being something which was an integral part of a historical Croatian territory -- the number of such persons is negligible. The people who thought that way, there weren't many people, but they did have their influence in political decision-making. But if we exclude them, then the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted to protect the people from genocide, from being killed, and they wanted to have a state in which the peoples, the ethnic groups, as well as individuals, would enjoy equal rights without domination, without assimilation, and they would consider a state of this kind, one along those lines, to be their rightful homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please: We left off discussing the BH army and their numbers. Do you know how many soldiers, how many men it numbered in December 1992 and January 1993? And did it undertake operations towards the Serbs at any time? For example, did it start to liberate Srebrenica, Gorazde, Eastern Bosnia, Western Bosnia, and so on and so forth? And focusing especially on the corridor.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the previous maps, we saw that there was an enclave around Bihac and that a corridor had been established by the Serb army and of the Serb army in Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we zoom in -- zoom out, please, Mr. Usher and the technical booth. Can we see the whole map now, please? Can we zoom out a bit? Thank you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the town of Bihac, there was an enclave, predominantly Muslim-populated, under the control of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army and one brigade of the Croatian Defence Council, under the command of General Santic, who was killed later on, and we never knew why or by whom. The Croatian volunteers from this bank of the Sava River tried to shut off the Serb corridor in order to lessen the pressure on the enclave, this enclave here, and Croatian territory, and they were defeated for several reasons. The first reason was the following: An order could not be issued to the regular forces of the Republic of Croatia to cross the Sava River and go to the assistance of the Croatian Defence Council there. The domestic forces were not sufficiently well organised and equipped to stand up to a well-organised and mighty army, the kind that the Serb army was, or rather, the Yugoslav People's Army. And the third reason was that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Praljak. Perhaps you'll be able to explain this better using the next map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, could you put the map on the ELMO, and we see the enclaves and all the rest on this map, which will facilitate the Trial Chamber. I'm not tendering this in any way, but just using the map to help us in understanding what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is where the corridor was narrowest, and apart from what I've already said, we kept looking for ways to have the Tuzla Corps of the BH army, who was very numerous and powerful, start out towards the HVO forces and cut off the corridor. By doing so, we would facilitate the military situation of Croatia here, and in western Slavonia and Croatia, moving down towards Knin, and the enclave populated by Muslims and Croats around the town of Bihac, and the pressure exerted by Serb forces via Kupres, Livno, going down towards Split on the coast. Unfortunately, at the end of 1992, the Muslim forces were politically and militarily in a very poor state, in poor shape. I have to say that this was due, in part, also to the fact that the international community showed a maximum degree of indecision and allowed the Serbs to do as they pleased. Sarajevo was under siege. There was no peace plan in the offing. The Serbs were just verbally condemned. Srebrenica and the Muslim enclaves in the eastern part towards the Drina River were under an encirclement. They were surrounded. And in all the negotiations we had with the BH army, we asked and expected to have a more forceful engagement, that is to say, to link up Srebrenica, Gorazde, and a deblockade for Sarajevo, or at least refuting the Serb guns, pushing them back further to prevent the massacre that was to befall the population. This was the state of affairs at the end of 1992. It was a very bad situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My question was: Do you know whether they had any operations against the Serbs in any area? Are you aware of anything like that? And I'm referring to the BH army.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Krsnik, after the fall of Jajce - and I was present there - once again under the leadership of the Croatian Defence Council, together we organised the defence of Travnik so that the Serb forces were unable to continue down the Lasva River Valley towards Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, we've now come to January 1993. How did relationships develop? The BH army, how did it develop? What was the situation? What were the developments? What happened next, to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that, faced with the situation of this kind, the BH army became increasingly and exclusively a religious army. I personally think that with so much suffering on the side of -- on the part of the Muslims, and with so many casualties and victims which they had in fighting -- in the fighting with the Serbs, this can be considered normal and reasonable and understandable. However, it is an undisputed fact. This observation is correct. Now, when a nation or ethnic group - and the Muslims were threatened with complete disarray, both as an army and as a form of political thought, political thinking - they were faced with their annihilation, then a metaphysical refuge for them was religion. This is an area of the soul and the spirit of the nation which remains as the last bastion, the last possible place of refuge, religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know that the BH army launched large-scale attacks in Central Bosnia at this time? Are you aware of that? Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did happen to know at the time that in the BH army, people were thinking and talking about the fact that the Serbs would be getting what they needed, and that the international community had taken the side of the Serbs and Serbia, and that they could only achieve something if they were to extend their territory towards the Croats. The Serbs, at the end of 1992, for their part, satisfied all -- had satisfied all their strategic and tactical and political goals as well, whereas we, in 1992 - I'm referring to the Croatian Defence Council and the political leadership - we no longer had any serious conflicts with the Serbs, because their attitude towards us -- that is to say, they had taken from us what they considered satisfied them. The Croatian Defence Council, as the weakest link in this three -- tripartite warfare had no reason or need or reason for opening up a front towards the Muslim forces. That would have been a political -- not a political -- a good political idea and completely devastating militarily. The Muslims, on the other hand, had to have a military success somewhere, had to have scored a military success somewhere. Then, and when the influx of an enormous number of members of different political options from the Islamic world, which we refer to as the Mujahedin, they began the Islamisation of the army. They began to introduce different customs and different laws, and they found a very fruitful ground for doing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, as we once did yesterday, I find that we are lapsing over into what the Prosecution would consider extensive opinion testimony not being given by an expert. This witness knows a lot, I'm sure, about what happened in the HVO. He's now, for the last few minutes, expressing strong opinions on the internal workings and philosophy and reform, or what have you, inside the ABiH, and there has Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. been no foundation offered as to how this witness can know this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as a rule, we only hear what the witness saw and did in those events, but we are very interested to know how the Croats and the Muslims finally fought with each other. This is the -- we are very interested in that, although it's forbidden by the Rules. But we'll let this witness go for a while. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Not only is the witness voicing his opinion, he also has knowledge of that, and when the witness speaks about the Mujahedin - and we shall go into that - you will also hear more explanations and more personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, tell us, are the Mujahedin regular members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which formations they belonged to, where are they, how many are they, and where do they engage in fighting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mujahedin are part of the regular strength of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is ample evidence about that, and it can be shown to the Court. The manner in which they arrived there were the humanitarian convoys. How? That we know. How? I know that. A humanitarian convoy would have 40 vans in disrepair, 40, and each one of them would have three or four escorts. And we were perplexed, why all the goods in 40 ramshackle vans had not been put into a trailer truck, and why people escorting those vans never went back? And even those vans never went back. We asked the authorities of the Republic of Croatia to bear this in mind, more than before, because we had clear military information that told us where they were, how they were trained, what kind of units they were forming, and what kind of war they wanted to wage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, did they add momentum to the conflict with Croatia? Did they speed up matters? What happened when they arrived? In which direction did the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina turn?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They significantly added to the momentum of the war. One of their bases was here between Novi Travnik - my eyesight is not what it was - and Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, Witness, you are talking about the events of the international humanitarian convoy. I just want to know did you saw -- did you see that? And what was the date, and where did you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I saw it with my own eyes, not once, because all those convoys entered -- arrived either from Ploce via Capljina, Citluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you please point to those places on the map?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ploce, Capljina, Citluk, Mostar, and then when the road was opened to Jablanica, and before that, Tomislavgrad, the road of salvation, which we built so that the refugees could get to here, because these roads could not be used, Uskoplje and onward. Not one Mujahedin could enter anywhere else except by taking these roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you are talking about the year?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1992 onward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you'll allow me, I realise fully, of course, it's the Court's question but I respectfully submit that the witness hasn't answered the Court's question, and this was exactly the part that relates back to the objection the Prosecution made a few moments ago. I think, if I understand your question, Mr. President, with all respect, you asked this witness to identify, very specifically, situations he saw with his own eyes or with his own personal perception of incidents where Mujahedin were smuggled into the country, so to speak, as it calls it, by means of humanitarian convoys. Now, respectfully, I submit to you, Mr. President, that question has not been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness, please be more concentrated and answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically, I saw, concretely, I wondered, and the military intelligence officers, I mean the officers in the army that I worked for, why so many small vehicles, why so many escorts in those small vehicles, why don't they go back, either the escorts or the vehicles? And we collected information on both. And those -- this information, even if partial, even if incomplete, can be found with many intelligence and security services of the western world, and I believe that Mr. Krsnik has it too. We requested for stricter control by the authorities of the Republic of Croatia because whenever we wanted to put an end to such an influx of warriors, who would then become a very poor army, and every time our ears would be boxed. Every time we would be accused that we were stopping international humanitarian convoys. Those same people in their camps, several times before the conflict, before the open conflict broke out, those men, on various occasions, captured my men and, for instance, once they captured Mr. Andric, who was in Bugojno. They stripped him naked and sent him down the road from Novi Travnik to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the year was and month, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was early 1993 or the end of 1992. I wouldn't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, tell us, please: Is there verified information when, in 1994, 1995, when the peace process started, did those people come back? Are the numbers of the passports, their names, and were all the western intelligence services informed about them, notably, the CIA?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik. We obtained photographs of many of them, their nationality, the information of their country of origin, the nationality of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was conferred upon them, the years of their birth, photographs. And since, regrettably, it became a matter of public interest in Croatia, in one such action --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go into private session, if we may, because these, after all, are matters that -- so, Your Honours, may we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask to see a videotape which marks the beginning of the conflict between the ABiH and the HVO, and you will see the tape and tell us about it. It is about the arrival of Mujahedin, which then set in motion things that we will see on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell us who are these men?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are Croats in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] From villages, should the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina expel all of them to enclaves? This means speeding, acceleration of war in Central Bosnia. Here, Mujahedin killed four escorts of a Zenica commander. Look at this. You will see that they were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. taking it out on those men. The number of bullets fired. Look at this. It is really a shocking scene. But these people were not killed as military. These were simply butchering of those men. We are seeing our killed, slayed, massacred men from Lasva. This is the Lasva Valley. These are the names: Zvonko Rajic, Franjo Rajic, Cegic [phoen], Stipo, Niko Kegelj, Vinko Kegelj, Dragan Kegelj, Pero Ljubisic, Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much. Can you stop the tape, please? Can you stop the tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, would you explain to Their Honours whether this was your voice on the tape, who gave me this tape, and on what occasion did you make these comments?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my voice, the first part. I prepared this tape for a TV programme in Zagreb, and in it I tried to explain the reasons at the beginning and the ascending spiral of the war between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us: When did this incident happen, and where did it happen? These three slain HVO soldiers, who did that and which year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were four soldiers. Those four soldiers were escorting the commander of a small formation of the Croat Defence Council from Zenica, and they were killed at a junction, at the crossroads in front -- outside, right outside Travnik. And those other men, those who were massacred, they came from a village in Central Bosnia. And the year is 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: On the tape -- I do not know whether it is in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'd ask that -- I object and would ask that we do better than "1993." These dates could be quite important. We started -- a few minutes ago we were in January 1993. Now we're just talking about sometime in 1993. And if the witness can assist us, Your Honour, I think the Court -- the Chamber needs to know with greater specificity when these events occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krsnik, could you ask some follow-up questions on this very issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, could you give us the month, at least. Perhaps you don't remember the date, but could you give us the month?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe I will be here tomorrow, so that meanwhile I can look at my tape, because there I have all the dates noted. I'm afraid to go wrong, and I really do not wish to make any such mistake, not to be accurate enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me help you. Was it before or after May 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was before May 1993. I think I can say with confidence that it was before May 1993, but for accuracy's sake, may I be allowed to answer this question tomorrow? I mean, there are just too many dates, and I really do not want to mention any that I'm not quite sure about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But, Mr. Praljak, you can make a small reminder for yourself. But tell us: Those men we saw in the woods, who and what are those men? What happened to them? What are they doing there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are expelled. They were expelled from a village in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, are they Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us: In view of your -- in the light of your personal experience and your post, would you know anything about the estimate of the number of Mujahedin, how were they organised, and which units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did they belong to, were they incorporated in?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They established their own brigade, which was called El Mujahedin, but they were also in other units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Their number grew as the war progressed, but with the relatively -- it can be relatively positively claimed that they were more than 5.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell us, did you give me a tape about Mujahedin, and how did you come by it? How did you obtain it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krsnik, I gave you several tapes. Those tapes were issued by the Mujahedin because they had their information office which recorded their promotional material, and they used to send it to Arab countries, inviting new members to join, because in those tapes, they claimed that the only kind of war waged in Bosnia was a religious war. I was given this tape by a combatant from Central Bosnia, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You don't have to give us his name, if you don't want to.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the technical booth to play the next tape, the clip from tape number 1? May I tell -- it is ID D1/50, actually, F. It is the F supplement. And the Arab translation will be ready in a day or two because half the tape is in Arabic and half of it is in the B/C/S language. The Arabic translation is ongoing and I thank the translators of the Tribunal for helping me and assisting me in having the text translated from the Arabic. The text in Arabic says the opposite of what the Prosecutor sets out in his indictment. As soon as the Arabic version is completed, I will furnish it to the Prosecution and Your Honours. May we see the tape and we'll comment after we see the footage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, here it says, "The El Mujahedin Detachment. Our road is the road of Jihad."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have a fast-forward here, please, because the tape is rather a long one? Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fast-forward, please, again. Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have a fast-forward again, please? Stop there, please. Stop the tape there, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Normally, of course, if they are good, Inshallah" --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Fighting for the honour -- for honour and for Allah's word to prevail. As far as kufra is concerned, hatred in the name of Allah, kufra and the struggle, until they are destroyed, Inshallah."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The El Mujahedin units in the seat -- at the headquarters in Zenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. May we continue, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The lives of the Mujahedin are the fraternal love for Allah, which has made the El Mujahedin unit the most powerful in the state. The fact that they have all gathered here from different parts in the world and towns in Bosnia is incomparable to anything else. When a doctor or professor leaves his comfortable home and the prosperity he lived in to come here, or a Saudi citizen or somebody from Yemen comes to Bosnia because he cannot take the killing of Muslims or the rape of their Muslim sisters, to come to Allah's call in the Jihad and along his road."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, but the text is fast. [Voiceover] And prepare as much strength and power to fight against them and horses for the struggle to frighten off Allah's and your foes, and others too. You do not know them, but Allah knows them very well. Everything that you use up along Allah's road you will be rewarded for, and you will suffer no injustice if you pursue along Allah's road. Praise be to Allah, Allah the almighty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have a fast-forward, please. Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] And set up a bastion that is impenetrable in the name of Allah. Praise be to Allah, who has united the brother Bosniaks of the Entereriya [phoen] and made them like a sabre to thwart the enemy, who wanted to destroy Islam and the Muslims in Bosnia. That is why the units are being joined by the faithful, the believers, from all parts of the world and from all parts of Bosnia. Let these suffoves [phoen] be guarantors of pride and victory for Islam and the Muslims. This is a brother of ours who is going to tell us how he prepared for this operation. Does he expect us to beat Allah's foes, and how far is he ready to fight? I think that Inshallah it will be as it has always been, and as long as we live. But in spite of all our preparations for battle, the main support to us is Allah's existence, and we rely on Allah's help and assistance, because Allah determines everything and exercises control over all the events, and he has already decided who the enemy is to be. But I'm always an optimist Inshallah that we will be victors, that we will be victorious and vanquish our enemies, because as far as I was able to see, our brothers, our brethren, have let the operation be led by Allah. And we have a lot of Ibadet and fervor for victory Inshallah. My message to my brethren, the Muslims, is to accept the faith, to return to the faith, to return to the Koran and the Sumet [phone]. Because we have been living here in Europe, we have been living under a communist system, we have lived under some newfangled ideas and concocted systems, but a Muslim has always been trodden over where there is no reliance on Allah and the true faith and a return to the fundamental premises of Islam, which is the Koran and the Sumet. So the Jihad, as proclaimed and as led by Elso Slabagaja Selum [phone], within those frameworks, and of course with even more fervor to kill all Allah's foes, because they are strong today and they are mightier than they have ever been. All right, brother. Thank you, brother. Allah be with you. Pray for us. Pray that Allah's faith prevails. Allah can see full well what they are doing. Our Bosa [phoen] from Kuwait says: Praise to the Allah. Fear Allah and do not die in any other way but as Muslims. Today is Friday, the Mubarak day. We are in the centre of our preparations. Praise and pray to Allah. And if you should die in the fighting, may Allah take you in and heal your wounds. The enemy side has modern technology and they have the advantage there, but we have the support of Allah, who assists his faithful slaves. Let me say to my brethren that we must rely on Allah and our faith and the humble qualities of the Emirs [phoen]. We have come here to help our brethren, the Muslims. We have had beautiful dreams, and one of our brethren told us that he dreamt that we were deployed with a man leading us in white clothing, with a cap on his head and with a beautiful dark beard, leading us to the trenches, and we followed him. He praised Allah's victory for Allah's assistance. We pray to Allah that we will have joyful tidings and that he will lead us in our battles Inshallah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have a fast-forward, please. Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have a fast-forward again, please. Fast forward again, please. Stop there, please. Thank you. We can stop there altogether for the moment, for the time being. Thank you. Thank you very much to the technical booth and everybody who assisted us from the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, could you now tell us, please, what you know about the events that we saw on the tape. From your personal knowledge, may we have your comments, please, to what we've just witnessed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of that footage, the images that were shown were the United Nations, the Pope, the UN troops, and all the rest that were shown, they were the enemy, the enemy to the faith, and the enemies of Allah and the Muslims. The torsion that you see, the contractions, facial grimaces on the faces of the people you saw were there because -- people's identities were being masked with face distortion on the footage. They were quite obviously important members of terrorist, Islamic organisations. Image distortion. The review that we saw of the brigades of the El Mujahedin, the review was conducted by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. He toured the troops, reviewed the troops. And by virtue of office, he was their commander. I think that I also recognised the commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina among the faces. He was later to become General Mahmuljan. At one point, we saw some captive Serbs, some Serb prisoners. We also saw the training centre, and the way in which the men were trained. In the speech that we heard, there was repetition of the fact that hatred was allowed in the name of Allah, was permitted in the name of Allah. Not only is it permitted, but that it is desirable too. And that in the name of Allah, they must kill those who are the enemies of Islam. And it is within that context that mention is made frequently of the word "Jihad," the Jihad. And the Jihad means a holy war. And Allah's foes are enumerated again, and mention is made of Europe and all new systems, which obviously are non-Islamic ones and are not founded upon the way of life proclaimed by the Koran. Mr. Izetbegovic himself asks briefly who the people assembled are, and in another section of the footage, the speaker that we can hear in the background, in "off," says that many professors --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, not to interpret what was said, I'm going to have the whole text translated, and the documents will speak for themselves, but I just wanted to hear your comments and some things that you knew of personally. But let's move on because our time is limited, and with the Court's indulgence, I have been -- my time has been extended today for the examination-in-chief, but we do have to end by the close of business today. So let's move on and let's focus on 1993 and tell us where you were in Bosnia, in Croatia. Did you return to Herzegovina? Could you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two landmark periods insofar as my tours of duty in Bosnia-Herzegovina are concerned. In 1993, in the former half of 1993, I went to Bosnia and Herzegovina whenever I could so as to help, either with the organisation or by taking over the command in one of the defence -- over one of the defence sectors, or so as to calm down the situation which was increasingly -- which increasingly looked like war between the Croat Defence Council and the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And when did you go back to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of July, 1993. I went down there again, and I was appointed the commander of the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sorry, you said "down there." What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to Croatia. I went back to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Don't. That's all right. Don't apologise. Just so, on the 27th of July, 1993, you went back to Herzegovina and you are appointed the HVO commander. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And tell us, what was the situation? What kind of a situation did you find there? Could you perhaps explain how were the forces deployed at the time? Perhaps we can use a map to make your explanations easier. This is ID D1/76. What was the situation then? How were the forces deployed? Where was the fighting going on, if there was any fighting going on at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation, in a manner of speaking, the situation for the Croat Defence Council, was bad. We were under attack from all directions, at all points of contact with the Muslims. The war had already started before I arrived there - I mean the open conflict - with all the elements Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of war. We had already lost various territories, territories from which we had been expelled, accompanied by series of crimes perpetrated by Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you be more specific as to the area?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Central Bosnia, Bugojno, Konjic. And then the Muslims embarked on their closing operation, which they called Neretva '93. What they wanted was to move down the Neretva valley and come out at Metkovic and then on to the coast. And there were already political speculations at the time that the Serbs might get the southern part of Croatia from Neum, and the Muslims at the same time thought they could get the area from Ploce to Neum. As the time went by in -- into fierce fighting, we managed to stop that offensive, to recover the positions that we at times lost along those directions, and defend the remains of the remains of the Croat enclaves in Central Bosnia, but without Kakanj, without Orasje, without Travnik, without Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, just briefly, how were the forces deployed? Will you please tell us the number of the exhibit and everything that is in Croatian and then let us comment on this map in just a few words.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is D1/76.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue means the Croat Defence Council. Green stands for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And red stands for the Army of the Republic of Serb Krajina. And the rest, I think, is self-evident. I don't see what else do I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And this map here, will you please be so kind as to -- so as to ensure the continuity and so that the Court can follow?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Exhibit D1/77, April, 1993, directions of operations of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, scenes of crimes of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, cleansing of Croat villages in the Neretvica valley. All the crimes that I've just pointed at have been documented, the villages were cleansed, their population expelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, partly for consistency's sake, I want the Prosecution position to be clear. As we have said from the beginning, we object to this evidence as irrelevant. It is not -- tu quoque is not a defence. The counsel has not tendered any other reason why this information is relevant to this case other than tu quoque. We said in our opening statement that crimes were committed on all sides. That has never been in dispute. This is not a defence to any issue in this case. Counsel has not tendered or proffered any reason why it's relevant. And we object to that. Secondly, we object to the broad-brush way that this information is being treated. Now, in the Prosecution case, the Prosecution has had to bring witnesses to establish crimes on the ground, elements and crimes and actual evidence. We have a witness here who, in a broad brush, has now said, without any basis or without any details, that Muslim crimes were committed at all these places. We object to this testimony, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, this is not the tu quoque defence. We are challenging the Prosecution thesis that the Croats or the Croat Defence Council attacked the Muslim people, that is, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This has nothing to do -- we are merely showing how Mostar happened, that is, how the conflict came about. We have to provide this explanation, and we cannot do it in one single sentence. These are crimes, and we're not interested in that. We have to go to the heart of the conflict and understand and explain why a broader conflict or, if you want to put it that way, why the war happened. And the Defence submits that as of the 16th of April onward, the HVO -- that was put to us, that the HVO attacked the Muslims and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We say no. What we submit is that the HVO and the Muslim -- and the Croat people was attacked before that and expelled them from the areas, and that then erupted in the all-out war in Mostar. And the only way we can prove our point is to explain it with witnesses who were there, with witnesses who held the highest-ranking positions, not by listening to the hearsay in Mostar, but having the situation where the high-ranking officials saw with their own eyes and about which they can testify before this Honourable Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, one brief comment. I won't belabour it further than we already have, except for this. I respectfully ask the Court to consider it this way: Assuming for the moment that anything that has been said in the last few minutes is true - and the Prosecution does not concede that that's true or that this version of events is correct - but assuming for the moment that it's true, is that a defence to the expulsion of Muslims from their homes in East Mostar? If that is true, is it a defence to the torture and beating of Muslim soldiers at the fish farm in Doljani? It's not relevant, Your Honour. We submit it is not relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott -- well, Mr. Scott, I think, you know, it's the time for a break. And Mr. Scott, I, in principle, quite agree with you that this Trial Chamber will not accept any evidence that is irrelevant, let alone that tu quoque defence, which we have been -- has been mentioned at the very beginning of this trial. But in this situation, we understand this witness is laying down the foundations for this case. There must be some instances which touch upon the wrongdoings of the other side. And we won't spend much time on that issue, Mr. Krsnik, because we have been sitting here for the whole morning. And I wonder how long are you going to take for this witness? Are you expecting us to sit until 7.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Your Honours, but of course not. I have three, four, five pages altogether, so about an hour and a half, and I believe that will then conclude my examination. As I said, I will try to do my best, but I'm trying -- so I'm trying to do my best to provide this Court with all the evidence, and we cannot explain why something happened unless we go back to the cause, because everything has a root somewhere. And this is the highest court on this planet, and that is the only way that we deem fit to provide evidence. The Defence said that it will never use tu quoque defence, but my learned friend doesn't understand. If he thinks that he has proven that there were expulsions and tortures and that these are already final judgements, then perhaps he would be entitled to a reaction such as this one, but not in this case. And even if I went along with my learned friend, who did that in our case with the background of the indictment, and we have to -- have to apply an individual approach to the indictment, and that is why this witness was called: Who did what. And even if the -- if I grant to the Prosecution that this and that happened in Mostar, but let us see who did it. I mean, it is up to him to prove who did that. It is on the Prosecution to prove who did it, and then we have to respond to the background of the indictment, which constitutes 90 per cent of the indictment, and only the rest are individual charges. I already said in my opening statement why do we have to go into things which are common knowledge simply because they are represented in a different way in the indictment? And therefore, we cannot but do that, and we are bringing the most relevant witnesses, witnesses who have absolutely their personal knowledge, who are all eyewitnesses, and we shall not have a single secondhand, hearsay witness. I've already said that, and we shall not bring any such witness here. Thank you very much, and I apologise for this rather long speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we are not quite satisfied with the proceedings this morning. It takes so much time. Remember that yesterday you told us altogether you need four hours for this witness. We have to move fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We don't have one hour and a half during our next sitting. I hope you could finish your direct examination in 30 to 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just say this: Here I have to address the testimony of Mr. Geld [phoen]. There are other documents. There are presidential transcripts. And this gentleman is an eyewitness. I really cannot plan the time. And I believe that this Honourable Court wishes to know about it, especially the presidential transcripts, Mr. Singara [phone], Jeremy Bowen. You remember BCC, don't you? And this gentleman personally, he personally can testify about this because he was an eyewitness. And I cannot skip various subjects. I'm really very sorry, but during the break I will try to focus on this. But finally I will have to ask the witness what he knows about my client, because that is also in the indictment. I will do my best, Your Honours. I will really do my utmost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll trust you, and during the break you reorganise your questioning concerning all those questions. We will rise until 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I merely wish to say that I will not have any questions in direct examination so that I can give my time to Mr. Krsnik, because I know how precious every minute is, and I have told him that I will not be using any time for direct examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I will now ask you to try to focus better and move on faster because we really have very little time left. So please try to make your answers as brief as possible. We have to reorganise slightly. I also had to do that, to go through all the topics that I had prepared. And I will now start by asking you about the structure of the HVO at the time when you arrived, as of the 28th of July -- 27th of July, 1993 onward. So let me ask you first, do you know Mr. Mladen Naletilic personally?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Have you known one another for a long time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've known one another since childhood. He was a year or two younger than I am, but we attended the same school in the same place, and we met again when he returned from abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know where and when the Convicts Battalion was established?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell the Honourable Court, if you have any direct knowledge, which rank did Mr. Mladen Naletilic enjoy in the HVO structure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladen Naletilic is not ranked in the HVO structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I will now show you a chart showing the HVO structure in 1993, and you will tell us whether it tallies with what you found when you got there, and I will invite you to comment on it and the structure and tell us where was who in -- on that chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, will you please help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And also I will show you Prosecution's Exhibit 532.1, which was done by the Spanish Battalion. So will you please have a look at it and compare the two? This is ID D1/82.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a more or less accurate chart of the HVO structure in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, because this is in Croatian, we do not have the translation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First comes the Supreme Commander, then the Defence Department, then below it is the Main Staff. The Military Police units are attached to the Defence Department. The Main Staff has command over four operative zones: Operative zone Mostar; Tomislavgrad operative zone; Vitez; Orasje operative zone. And directly tied to the Main Staff are the units attached to the Main Staff, and special purpose units and professional units are directly related to the Main Staff through the Defence Department. And then on, that is upward, to the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, but that is clear. Tell us what are the special purpose units or have you heard of the term "ATG"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the term "ATG." These are mostly units which would go to the front line at a particular point in time, perform a task and then go back home, in point of fact, because there were no barracks. And in those instances when they stayed on the front lines, then they would be subordinated to the commander of that particular front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that you mention it, could we go into private session, Your Honours, please? Because some names perhaps will be mentioned, and I'd rather not have them spoken in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time of my command, while I was the commander of the Croat Defence Council, I never once participated, nor did I see Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, plan, command, or perform a military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did he issue orders to you, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, he did not issue orders to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did he perhaps transmit some orders to you? Did he coordinate? Was he a coordinator between the Croatia and the HVO, the Croatian state and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'd call such a thesis and such claim preposterous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Mladen Naletilic present at the meetings of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was never at those meetings, and it wasn't his to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you ever see him plan an HVO action?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were together only during the liberation of the hill above Mostar that I already mentioned, Orlovac, but it wasn't he who planned it. It was simply the authority that he wielded, the authority that he enjoyed before the war, as a Croat patriot, in Communist Yugoslavia, so he -- so the combatants of the unit held him in high esteem. And in the planning of the liberation of Orlovac, I was present when that plan was drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell us: Which year was it, the Orlovac action?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was May. It was May. It was May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, do you have any knowledge whether -- about Rastani on the 29th of September, 1993? Do you know anything about this action and what happened there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time I held the office of the commander of the Croat Defence Council. In Rastani, on that date, an attack of the Muslim forces was rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Perhaps I can help you with a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usher, can you please be so kind as to help me? This is ID D1/86 and ID D1/87.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The city of Mostar, Rastani. The attack of Muslim forces came along the right bank of the Neretva to go around Mostar, but the Home Guard units and the brigade successfully thwarted this attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Perhaps we should use another map to show that. ID D1/87. Will you please tell us what does it say in Croatian so that we can follow?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The situation on the 23rd of September, 1993, Rastani." The red -- the forces in red are the units of the Muslim forces the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this is the confrontation line, when the attack was rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you tell us which units took part in this on the side of the Croat Defence Council and which units were involved on the side of the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the brigades -- there were two brigades in Mostar. One was Dobrobrodska [phoen] the Home Guards Brigade, as we called it. And another one. I cannot really tell you now offhand which Muslim units were attacking because it would be going into too much detail for the position that I occupied at the time. I know that I commanded the units which succeeded in stopping the attack, and which would have, had it succeeded, placed Mostar in a very difficult position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did the Croatian army, Croatian units, participate in the defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, counsel, there were no Croatian troops, troops from the Republic of Croatia, in that defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what about the Convicts Battalion units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Convicts Battalion was not there. There was the Home Guards Brigade from Mostar, whether the first or the second, I wouldn't really be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My colleague reminds me that you've already answered my question whether the Croatian troops participated in that action and you said not here but -- and no where else, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
