utterances.text: Well, with regard to the questions that we already considered about the never-ending participation of the Croatian troops in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that to not -- to leave the impression that they did not participate here but did elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Praljak, but we have to check the transcript. My colleague warns me that the transcript is not quite clear, so I must ask you explicitly. Did the Croatian army participate in any action at that time, before or after? Are you aware, therefore, of any action, that it took an active part in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said exactly and precisely. I have quoted two instances during that war, when, how and how many soldiers of the Croatian army were present in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I have nothing else to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, very much, Mr. Praljak. We have simply to make things clear for the record, so I apologise if I have to ask you certain things repeatedly. Tell us, did the intervention units -- can intervention units use prisoners if they go into attack, for instance, as a live shield, or do they take some prisoners or -- and use them for something, for some purpose?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krsnik, nobody can do that, not only intervention units. Nobody can do that. Nobody can have -- can keep prisoners outside the organisation. Nobody may use prisoners as a human shield. And if that happened somewhere, that was then the violation of the law of war and the violation of all the rules, of all the regulations that we managed to not only to adopt but to enforce and control the enforcement in spite of all the chaos of all the disarray that reigned at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Praljak, did you have talks with foreign representatives at the time, representing the international communities who were down there? Did you take part in any peace initiatives? And if so, which international representatives did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many, as we -- our time is limited, let me just say many. In Medjugorje, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1993, with Lord Owen, President Franjo Tudjman, the President of the Presidency -- of the rump Presidency of the Muslims, Alija Izetbegovic, various commanders and so on. With the Spanish Battalion, representatives of the Spanish Battalion, there were regular meetings with them. Then General Bricmont, the Commander-in-Chief of the international forces, we had meetings with him. With Mr. Garrod, with journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Which journalists did you talk to, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a journalist at the BBC, I've forgotten his name, but there was a rather sharp verbal conflict between the two of us. And then we -- I continued the conversation with Mr. Garrod. I also spoke to Mr. Gutman who received the Pulitzer Prize sometime later, and Mrs. Sally Baker, she wrote a book about it all. And many, many others. I can't go through them all now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did the BBC journalists, did they have to ask permission to film and where did they do their filming?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did ask permission to film the eastern part of Mostar and I asked that before they go into the eastern part of Mostar, that they should strike a balance between the facts as they stand and present the truth in a well-balanced way, and that they should inform the people of the situation in -- downstream from the Neretva, around Konjic and so on. We considered - and I did so personally as well - that - and I still consider that today to be true - that there was a propaganda war being waged against us at the time, so that the Muslims, as victims of the Serb aggression, were treated as if we had launched an aggression on them too. That was how the situation was portrayed, to my mind. After talking to Mr. Garrod, I managed -- we let the gentlemen from the BBC go and film Eastern Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How did they get to Eastern Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were escorted by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: You mean from the western part to the eastern part, along with your escort; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Praljak, I'm going to show you a document now, the number is D1/32. It is a Prosecution exhibit, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could I ask the usher for his assistance? D1/32 is the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The document was compiled by the international force and it pertains to all important people in the HVO. So could you take a look at it carefully? Could you look through the document, please -- or shall we do this together? Let's leaf through it quickly. Is Mate Boban's position correctly stated? And I think you have the text in English, unless I'm very much mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, could this document be put on the ELMO so we could have a look at it? Because we don't have this document at our hands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says Mate Boban, and everything is correct for Prlic. For -- incorrect for Topic. Bruno Stojic, correct. Slobodan Bozic, correct. Branko Kvsic, I'm not sure. I don't know this next one. I'm not sure about the next one. He was chief of the security service, that one there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Does that mean that is incorrect, then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Incorrect, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now what does the word "police" mean here? Is it police or what?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is "police."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Then it is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Gagro, incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, could you -- when you say something is correct or incorrect, could you read out the name, please, first?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stjepan Kresic, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: If somebody does not exist within the structure, then tell us that, too.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jozo Maric, incorrect. Leica, doesn't exist. I don't know who he is. Ratko Peric, yes. Bishop, correct. Milivoj Petkovic was my deputy. He wasn't policy director or anything. Milivoj Petkovic was a brigadier at the time and I was a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So that means that is not correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That wasn't correct, and I'm not Praljac with a C, I'm Praljak with a K. And I was commander, yes, that's correct. Zarko Tole, Chief of Staff, correct. Pero Zelenika, not correct. Lucic, Ivica, that's the one -- previous one. And it's Ivica with a "C," not Ivika with a K. Correct. He was in charge of security and the police. Milenko Lasic, correct, commander of the zone. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you please read the name out, first?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivan Andabak, correct. Nedeljko Obradovic, Mojmir Primorac; correct. There are some missing here, some parts missing. For example, Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It says "General Staff."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's another Naletilic. He was in the Main Staff, a certain person with the surname Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, I have sufficient copies. Could you hand this around, please? I think the Prosecution has a copy of this document. Hand one copy to the witness, please. Could you place it on the ELMO? The Prosecution has a copy, has been provided with a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Is that the man in question with the surname Naletilic? Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Naletilic who was in the Main Staff of the HVO, General Staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is ID D1/88. Thank you, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, is that a document that was produced by a member of the UN Monitoring Mission, European Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I thought he explained to us that it was really telephone numbers of people who were useful to them, and nothing more than that. I thought he explained that to us. Is that a different list?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. It's the same list, but it went via the Prosecution, the investigator of the Prosecution, Mr. van Hecke. We got it by way of him. Not only -- it wasn't only telephone numbers, but who was who in the HVO, plus telephone numbers. And Mr. van Hecke testified to that. He was the main investigator of the Prosecution team. And if you remember, at the time, when I asked him where Mr. Naletilic was and whether it was this particular Mr. Naletilic. I asked Mr. van Hecke that question during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I must be thinking of a different list. If you give me the Prosecution number of that, I'll be able to look it up in my own files when I go back to the office. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but I do not have the number of the Prosecution document. But I have the numbers, the basic numbers. But you'll find it difficult to find your way with them. But perhaps my colleagues, my learned colleagues across the well, can help me. But we tendered it, and the number was D1/32. We introduced it on the basis of D1/32, on the 7th of November, 2001, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to take up your valuable time. We can look it up later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're stopped on exhibits, the Prosecution would assist -- would appreciate some assistance on the foundation, the source of Exhibit D1/88, this document supposedly about this other Naletilic. There's been no information as to the source or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to be frank, I can't say, but I think it was within the frameworks of a request we made to the authorities in Mostar, and as far as I remember, it says here that it is the file of a person who was replaced. It was an ID card. We asked MUP Mostar for a lot of information, and this is taken from their files, which every citizen in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina has in the police force. That is to say, the police have files which they keep for their personal identification cards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, since you've seen the Croatian language, we don't understand the first line of the words. Maybe you can assist us by translating them into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says: Card of issued or replaced personal ID, personal identification card. And this was the system introduced in the former Yugoslavia and has prevailed to today. Each citizen has one personal identification number, plus his name and surname, first and last name, the last name of his parents, with the maiden name of the mother, date of birth, place of birth, municipality of birth, state. National affiliation or ethnicity, it says "Croat." Profession, it says "professor." Education, it says "higher education." Residence, Siroki Brijeg, municipality of Siroki Brijeg. Address, date of issuance of the ID, and valid until the 2nd of October, 2005. Issued the 2nd of October, 1995, valid until the 2nd of October, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me ask you again, Witness: Do you know this man, and do the facts correspond to the situation as it stands?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the gentleman, and as to the first and last name, they are correct; they correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. I keep having to look at the clock. I apologise if this is a little disconcerting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now see a tape, and I'm going to ask you about the problems you encountered down there when you were the commander, what you did to organise the people, et cetera. Could I ask the technical booth to play the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And could you tell us the date and the place, please, when this was filmed, who filmed it, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Soldiers, you're going to listen to me, and the rest of you too. We're not talking about love here. I have received eight trucks. I received eight trucks this morning. We have to go to the Croatian people in Vares and pull out eight dead bodies from Mostar. It's not a question of love. We have examined the convoy, checked the convoy. We have to transport people up there. What happened, happened. The rest will do their duty, their jobs, in order to feed the people in Vares, in Zepce, in Vitez. We have to let this go by. There's no question about that. Gentlemen, soldiers, move away from there, and the convoy has to go through. Shut up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can stop the tape there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, tell us when this happened, where it happened, whether there were similar situations with other humanitarian aid convoys. The place and time, please, where this was filmed and when.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the summer of 1993. The place is Citluk. The people had stopped the APC transporters and the convoy carrying humanitarian aid moving towards Eastern Mostar, because the people felt in jeopardy and that they found it difficult to accept the fact that in an imposed -- a war imposed on us by the Muslims, we allowed convoys to pass through, and as I said previously, carrying weapons too. The truth is -- it is true that they allowed convoys to pass through towards our enclaves in Eastern Bosnia too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: There were nine dead bodies mentioned that had to be exchanged. What was that about? What was that reference to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this was all linked up in that war. We were able to -- we would be given the bodies once the convoy had passed through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But the civilians were Croats, were they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the civilian were Croats, and I myself was there as the commander, and I had to intervene against the people, in opposition to the people and the will of the people, in actual fact. I had to get up on the APC itself, on the vehicle, and escort them through to Eastern Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I saw that there was no rank insignia on your clothing. Were there ranks in the HVO? If there were, tell us when they were introduced, or tell us generally when ranks were introduced and what the command structure and what commanding consisted of in the HVO at that time.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have ranks in the HVO. We had insignia denoting a command of a military structure, the commander of the Main Staff, for example, the deputy commander of the Main Staff, et cetera, the zone commander, the brigade commander, and so on and so forth. Ranks were introduced quite a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you had commanders, from the lowest unit to the highest unit; is that right? Am I reading you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I started asking you yesterday, and I said I'd continue today, whether you personally had talks with the president of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm going to show you some transcripts now. Would you take a look at them carefully, study them carefully, and tell us whether they correspond to the gist of your conversation with the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first transcript is PT32. It is marked PT32. I apologise. I omitted to give a number for the tape. It is ID D1/89, and I'm very grateful to my colleague for reminding me of that. Thank you. The conversation was allegedly held on the 22nd of January, 1992, in the presidential palace.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is too short a time for me to be able to say whether this is authentic or not. There's too much of it. I would have to read through the entire text. I was present at the meeting. Now, what it says here from start to finish, I can't really say. It was seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. To save time, I'm certain that my learned colleague will be asking questions about that during the cross-examination, but do you perhaps recall a conversation you had on the 15th of September, 1993 - and the number of that document is PT9 - also with President Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th of September? Which year did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In 1993, held at the presidential palace, Presidnicki Dvori [phoen].

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you without the text that on the 15th of September I was in Rama, Prozor, on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Actually, I was -- because that's when the Muslim crime in Uzdol took place, so I was there on the 15th of September. That's where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: It says here that you attended a meeting, and that you weren't in Rama, and that you talked to the president of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krsnik. I say when I know a date and I say when I don't. There was a great crime that took place in the village of Uzdol, Prozor on the 15th of September, and I know I was there, because I issued an order to the Croatian forces to liberate Uzdol and the people who were blocked in a school, some hundred-odd people who would have suffered the same fate as the 30-odd people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who attacked whom?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crime committed in Uzdol was committed by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: How many civilians were killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirty-something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you were there then?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All right. I won't question you any more about that, because it says here not only that you were present but that you took part in the discussion.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm quite certain of where I was on that particular date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And this brings us to our last transcript and document, the alleged meeting held on the 5th of November, 1993, at the Vila Dalmacija in Split, and the number of that document is PT12. Could you leaf through that one, please, and tell us where you were, whether you were there? Did you ever get a copy of the record?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were you aware that it was being recorded when you went to see the President?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Split, no, no, I'm certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Here it says, you will see, "recorded," and every record, every single minutes has that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I cannot really testify to the authenticity of these documents. Your Honours, I'm really sorry but I cannot say anything about this. I would have to read it first and see whether it would reflect what I retained in my memory, but just by looking at it, I cannot say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, well, well, perhaps you will have an opportunity during the cross-examination. You will have time and you will be able to read it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you have time, I'm quite ready now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do not have any more time. The Court was kind enough as to give me some more time but I have spent it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I have your leave to give these texts to the witness so that he can read it all this afternoon? There are very many pages, very -- very many pages and it's very important for us. I can give him the copy which I was given so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: In reality, your witness should have seen all these documents before you raised the questions, because one of the main rules in cross-examination is you don't ask a question to which you don't know the answer. So strictly speaking, this witness really should have had an opportunity to see all this material before. Are you saying, Mr. Krsnik, you don't know whether he's going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake. Entirely my mistake. I simply didn't manage to do it all. I had a month, thanks to your kindness, but it was 60 witnesses and I had to prepare them. And you see how much time I spent here in the courtroom. Can you imagine how much time I had to spend talking to those people, interviewing them, talking them into coming here? Yes, I failed to do that, and it is my mistake, but with your leave, I will give the -- I will give the witness to read it. If not, then it can be done yesterday, because I'm quite sure that my learned friends will also address this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: In what I said there, one of the main rules in cross-examination should be one of the main rules in examining a witness is that you don't ask, not cross-examination. I obviously said that incorrectly. But as you've finished with this witness, you just want him to read these documents in order that he may be ready for any questions which Mr. Scott might have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One or two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, your request is granted, Mr. Krsnik. You may furnish this document to your witness. I hope this is your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Two, two questions more, very brief. My colleagues warn me which questions I must not forget to put.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Many witnesses here in the courtroom affirmed that at the Heliodrom, there were Croatian -- units of the Croatian army called the Tigrovi, Tigers, and Thunders -- Thunderbolts, Gromovi. Would that be correct? And I have an order here, which is marked ID D1/84.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your first question, Mr. Krsnik? My answer is Croatian army units, as organised formations, which the Croatian army might have dispatched to the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina do not exist. There do exist volunteers who, from the Croatian army, went to join units of the Croat Defence Council, because they, as we have already stated, they had been born in that territory. From the territory they had gone to the Croatian army. And Bosnia and Herzegovina was both their homeland and their fatherland. Some of them, notwithstanding strict orders to remove the patches of the Army of the Republic of Croatia, for psychological reasons and because we did not have such an organisation to enforce it all, went on wearing those patches, but only as individuals, in their individual capacity, and not as members of the Army of the Republic of Croatia. And this is attested to by this order, among other things, which says that the volunteer units will be received -- when we say "units," then these are very small groups of men. And that these volunteer units will be received by Colonel Ivica Primorac, who will take care of their accommodation and logistic support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. And item 2?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Volunteer units arriving there will be accommodated in the barracks at the Heliodrom. And here, mention is made of 90 men and a unit for Bosanski Brod is announced of volunteers again, which unfortunately never turned up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And item 3?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The use in -- the use in combat of such volunteer groups shall be regulated by the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council. In other words, I command these men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who signed this order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was signed by General Matic, Stanko Matic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And his office was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it says here. Yes, yes, of course, Deputy Chief of the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council. I would have known that even without anything in writing. Mr. Krsnik showed me Mr. Garrod's report, and I confirm that it is correct, truthful and honest, and that reflects honestly, properly and authentically the situation, described the situation correctly and the problems which the BBC television team had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The document that Mr. Praljak volunteered the information is P611.1. Oh, we've skipped now over very many things. My last question, since you were the commander at the time, document marked P611 -- P611, which says the 23rd of September, 1993, one has a seal, the other one doesn't, and it says, Defence Minister Bruno Stojic. I don't know if this is his signature, so I will show it to you to tell us. So on the 23rd of September, he was commended for valour and military prowess in the fighting around Rastani and at the hydro power, and it says, headed -- the unit headed by Commander Tuta for the -- and for the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please place it on the ELMO? Because he's reading a text which the interpreters do not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the contribution in the liberation of Rastani, the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because the interpreter could not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say whether this is Mr. Stojic's signature, because too much time has gone by. But it wasn't really all that common, and I do not know how a minister can commend a military unit. The only way that it could have come about was that I had given the foundation for him, and I did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But was there any action in Rastani before that? I mean before the 23rd of September, because as far as I know, and I stand to be corrected, on the 23rd of September, the action was still underway.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd of September, the action was not over yet, but as far as I know, it wasn't in Rastani. There was a strike by Muslim forces and the commander, by the very fact, by the nature of his command, had to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But were there any counter -- were there any such strikes before the 23rd of September that you remember?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my very last question, but you still owe us a comment on this SpaBat structure of the HVO, and that would be my last and my closing and concluding question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I cast a look at it, and unfortunately, this is a very dilettante piece of work and this is the mildest way to describe this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is all, Your Honours. Thank you very much for your indulgence, patience and understanding. On behalf of the whole Defence team, I really have to say that we are -- I cannot explain how highly we appreciate the fact that you allowed us to extend our examination. Thank you very much indeed. And I apologise, the number of this document. [In English] This document, I would like to see the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I'm afraid that we have to call you back tomorrow morning for the cross-examination. So the usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, do you know how many hours you spent on this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About six hours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. I believe more than that. It's too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are measuring the time but -- see how wrong I was, Your Honours. I didn't run -- I did not produce five tapes and I'll have to do that with some other witnesses. At the time we were preparing the summary, we were in Siroki Brijeg. You know how honest I am with you. I simply had no idea how long it would take, with all the objections, with all the tapes, with the documents, and so on and so forth, but the responsibility rests with me, and I do apologise. I really had no idea how much I would need for witnesses like this one. But believe me, that will not be the rule. Perhaps it will hold true of the first five or six witnesses, and then we shall enter the second stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you will indulge me literally one minute, first off, by our records, just so the point is clear, we calculate approximately 6 hours 40 minutes. In terms of, Your Honour, we would ask about the next five, to confirm the exact order, in light of the changes that we have experienced. If we could be, please, assisted by tomorrow morning with confirmation of the next five defence witnesses, the names and exact order in which they would appear, we would be much appreciative. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, since this is the first few witnesses, and since it's a very important witness in your case, and since we still have time, so we let you go for about six hours, but that should never happen with the next few witnesses, because the time at our disposal is so limited. We have to conduct our trial in a very efficient way. The second issue is that we believe that it is the obligation on your part to furnish all the documents and the names of the witnesses of the Defence counsel. We had the ex parte hearing and this Trial Chamber will consider your request upon your written motions, but until now, we received nothing in this respect. Thirdly, Mr. Krsnik, since so many documents was used in your direct examination, we request you to submit to us a list of all those documents you used during your direct examination before tomorrow morning so that we could see which document is about what incident. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. We shall do that. We filed a motion this morning. It had to do with the ex parte. Then yesterday some changes took place. The Prosecution somewhat modified their views. We informed you and we filed the motion this morning. And as regards witnesses, we -- tomorrow morning -- the Prosecution will have the list of witnesses faxed this afternoon, with all the changes, because of the witness's illness and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We will rise until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of April, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
